proposal.reactor_type: PFA capillary coil reactor (with in-line PEEK static mixer at inlet), immersed in a thermostatted oil/water bath; optional SiC plate reactor as scale-up alternative
proposal.tubing_material: PFA (perfluoroalkoxy) - chemically inert to HNO3/acetic acid, rated to 150-200 C
proposal.light_setup: none - thermally driven electrophilic aromatic substitution, no photochemical activation required

streams.contents: aniline derivative (assumed protected/acetylated or protonated form to survive strong HNO3, as per original batch chemistry)
streams.solvent: glacial acetic acid (assumed 'industrial batch solvent' - common for aromatic nitration; state as explicit assumption since original text did not name it)

streams.contents: concentrated/fuming nitric acid (assumed 90% HNO3, delivering ~4.5 M effective concentration)

proposal.mixer_type: Low-dead-volume PEEK T-mixer or slit-plate micromixer, followed by short pre-cooled mixing zone before entering heated coil
proposal.mixing_order_reasoning: Substrate stream is introduced into the nitric acid stream (rather than the reverse) through a T-mixer to ensure the aromatic substrate is never locally exposed to large excess neat HNO3 pockets, which would promote oxidative side reactions and runaway exotherm. Premixing occurs at 0-5 C before the combined stream enters the heated 60 C reaction coil, decoupling fast micromixing from thermal initiation.
pre_reactor_steps: Chill both feed reservoirs and feed lines to 0-5 C using a jacketed pump head or ice bath to suppress premature reaction at the mixer
In-line 2 micron filtration of both streams to prevent clogging of the micromixer/capillary
Degassing of nitric acid stream to remove dissolved NOx that could nucleate bubbles and disrupt flow
post_reactor_steps: In-line quench into a stirred vessel of ice-water/aqueous NaHCO3 (or Na2CO3) immediately after the BPR to neutralize residual HNO3 and stop over-nitration
Continuous liquid-liquid phase separation (membrane separator or settling coil) to isolate the organic dinitro product
Aqueous acid stream directed to neutralization/waste treatment (NOx scrubbing) before disposal
proposal.chemistry_notes: This is a classic electrophilic aromatic dinitration. The exotherm from mono- then di-nitration is substantial and difficult to control in a stirred batch reactor over 4 h at 60 C, risking thermal runaway, over-oxidation, and inconsistent regioselectivity. In flow, the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of a narrow-bore PFA coil or SiC plate reactor allows rapid heat removal, permitting the same 60 C setpoint to be held uniformly, which should allow residence time compression from 240 min (batch) to an estimated 20-40 min while maintaining or improving the reported 89% yield. Excess HNO3 (assumed 4-5 equiv total) drives full dinitration; large excess also helps suppress mononitro intermediate accumulation.

stage_1_precool_mix.purpose: fast micromixing, minimize premature reaction before controlled thermal zone

stage_2_reaction_coil.purpose: bulk dinitration reaction, controlled via bath temperature and BPR-set pressure

stage_3_quench.purpose: stop reaction, neutralize acid, prevent further nitration/decomposition

reasoning_per_field.residence_time_min: Batch used 4 h; flow intensification (fast/efficient mixing and heat transfer) typically allows 5-10x reduction. 30 min chosen as a conservative first estimate pending empirical optimization.
reasoning_per_field.flow_rate_mL_min: Total 2.0 mL/min (1:1 stream ratio) selected as a lab-scale value compatible with standard syringe/HPLC pumps and capillary tubing; can be scaled linearly by numbering-up.
reasoning_per_field.temperature_C: Held at 60 C to match the batch protocol's proven reaction temperature; flow reactor's superior heat transfer makes this setpoint safer to maintain than in batch.
reasoning_per_field.concentration_M: 0.5 M substrate assumed as a typical practical loading for nitration chemistry balancing solubility and reaction rate; not specified in original protocol, so treated as an assumption.
reasoning_per_field.BPR_bar: 10 bar back-pressure regulator maintains single liquid phase, suppresses NOx off-gassing/bubble formation at 60 C, and allows safe operation above the atmospheric boiling point of dissolved gases without solvent-specific superheating.
reasoning_per_field.reactor_type: PFA coil selected for chemical compatibility with strong HNO3/acetic acid media and ease of immersion in a thermostatted bath at lab scale; SiC plate reactor (e.g., Corning AFR) noted as an industrial scale-up option for superior heat exchange.
reasoning_per_field.tubing_material: PFA chosen over stainless steel or FEP because concentrated HNO3 is corrosive to metals and FEP has lower thermal/chemical durability at 60 C over extended runs.
reasoning_per_field.tubing_ID_mm: 1.0 mm ID balances adequate heat transfer surface-to-volume ratio with acceptable pressure drop and reduced clogging risk from any precipitated nitro-product.
reasoning_per_field.reactor_volume_mL: Calculated directly from residence_time_min x flow_rate_mL_min (30 min x 2.0 mL/min = 60 mL) to ensure internal consistency.
reasoning_per_field.streams: Two-stream design mirrors the batch two-component system (substrate + HNO3); concentrations and equivalents are assumptions since the original protocol did not specify stoichiometry or solvent identity.
reasoning_per_field.mixer_type: Low-dead-volume mixer needed to achieve rapid, uniform contacting of two liquids of different viscosity/density before the thermal zone, minimizing hot-spot formation.

literature_analogies: Continuous nitration of aromatic substrates using Corning Advanced-Flow (SiC) reactors, demonstrating improved safety and yield versus batch nitration (Ducry & Roberge, Org. Process Res. Dev. 2005; Braune et al., 2008)
DSM/Corning continuous nitric acid nitration case studies showing residence time reduction from hours (batch) to minutes (flow) with comparable or improved yield
General flow-chemistry exothermic nitration literature emphasizing PFA/PTFE or SiC reactors with in-line quench for HNO3-mediated reactions
safety_flags: Highly exothermic electrophilic nitration - risk of thermal runaway if cooling fails; continuous online temperature monitoring at multiple coil points recommended
Concentrated/fuming HNO3 is strongly corrosive and oxidizing; use PFA/PTFE wetted parts only, avoid stainless steel contact with neat HNO3
Potential NOx gas evolution - reactor must be operated under back-pressure to remain liquid-phase; downstream NOx scrubbing required at vent/quench stage
Dinitroaromatic products may be shock-sensitive/explosive on concentration or drying - handle post-quench stream with care, avoid evaporation to dryness in-line
Blast shield and remote operation recommended during initial residence-time and stoichiometry optimization runs
Assumed solvent (acetic acid) and stoichiometry are not confirmed from the original protocol - verify experimentally before scale-up
